title: The outside passed pawn
summary: The pawn far from everything drags the enemy king away, and your king captures the pawns on the other side.
part.decoy.title: The pawn that drags the king
part.decoy.summary: Equal material, but one passed pawn far away: it becomes a decoy and your king does the rest.
part.pawnFirst.title: The decoy goes all the way
part.pawnFirst.summary: While the target cannot run, the pawn moves first: every step takes the enemy king farther away.
part.escort.title: The decoy near the king
part.escort.summary: When the decoy is close to the enemy king, it does not walk alone: it advances with check, with your king always beside it.
part.down.title: The race after the decoy
part.down.summary: A pawn down: one pawn holds two, the decoy drags the king, and in the end the kings race. Count first.
part.defense.title: On the other side: stopping the outside passer
part.defense.summary: When the outside passer is your opponent's, your king goes after it at once, without stopping for a free pawn.
part.protected.title: Against the protected passed pawn
part.protected.summary: The king cannot capture a protected passed pawn. Against it, the outside passer becomes a target.
part.pass.title: Trade or pass
part.pass.summary: With two pawns against one, do not trade: go past and create a protected passed pawn.
part.fischer.title: Fischer against Larsen
part.fischer.summary: Denver, 1971: Fischer trades bishops because the pawn ending is won. Then the rules and a position to play to the end.
step.t_decoy: Equal material: each side has two pawns and one passed pawn, White's on a4, Black's on e5. Both kings are in the centre. Why is this winning for White, and what is the plan?
step.t_decoy.hint1: Compare the distances. The e5 pawn is close to both kings. The a4 pawn is far from everything.
step.t_decoy.hint2: If the black king goes after the a-pawn, how long is it away from e5 and g4? And what does your king do in that time?
step.decoyWhy: The a4 pawn is far from everything. When it moves, the black king has to run after it, or it queens. But the king cannot be in two places: while it goes to the a-file, my king goes to e5 and g4 and captures what was left there. The a-pawn is a decoy. It will be captured, but it takes the black king far away with it. That is why it is called an outside passed pawn: what matters is the distance, not the pawn.
step.d_decoy: Watch the whole plan. Notice where each king is when the a-pawn falls.
step.d_decoy.m1: 1.a5. The pawn moves, and the black king already has to think about it: in three moves it queens.
step.d_decoy.m2: 1...Kc5. Black goes after the pawn. If not, it queens.
step.d_decoy.m3: 2.a6. One more step: every step takes the black king further into the corner.
step.d_decoy.m4: 2...Kb6. The black king catches the pawn. But look where it is: on b6, three files away from e5.
step.d_decoy.m5: 3.Ke4. I let the a-pawn go: it has done its job. The e5 pawn is undefended.
step.d_decoy.m6: 3...Kxa6. Black captures the decoy, far away in the corner.
step.d_decoy.m7: 4.Kxe5. A pawn for a pawn, but my king is in the centre and Black's is on the a-file. Next the g4 pawn falls, and the g3 pawn queens.
step.decoyMove: Your turn. Use the a-pawn as a decoy and, at the right moment, take the king to the other side.
step.decoyMove.hint: First the a-pawn moves and drags the black king. When the black king is close to it, go after the e5 pawn.
step.decoyMove.done: That's it. The black king is tied to the a-file, and your king has reached the e5 pawn. Now capture and win.
step.t_pawnFirst: Now Black's passed pawn on d4 is blocked by your king, and the g5 pawn threatens your kingside. The black king on f4 is eyeing f3. Capturing d4 right away looks natural. Is it the best, or is there a better plan?
step.t_pawnFirst.hint1: Can the d4 pawn run away? If not, it can wait.
step.t_pawnFirst.hint2: If your king leaves d3 to capture, who is watching the f3 pawn?
step.t_pawnFirst.hint3: The farther up the a-pawn is, the farther the black king has to go to fetch it.
step.pawnFirstWhy: In the first part the decoy moved two squares and my king left at once. Here, leaving too early throws the win away. The d4 pawn cannot move: my king on d3 stands in front of it. It cannot run, so it can wait. First the a-pawn moves, and every step forces the black king to leave f4 and head for the a-file. Only then do I capture d4.
step.pawnFirstMistake: First, the natural mistake: 1.Kxd4? The black king answers 1...Kxf3, and the g5 pawn becomes passed, with nobody in front of it. My king tries to come back: 2.Kc3 g4 3.Kd2 g3 4.Ke1 g2, and the pawn queens next move, with the black king on f3 guarding its path. The a-pawn never even moved.
step.d_pawnFirst: Now the right order: pawn first, king later.
step.d_pawnFirst.m1: 1.a4! The pawn moves. Capturing d4 can wait, because it cannot run.
step.d_pawnFirst.m2: 1...Ke5. The black king protects d4, but it leaves f4: now it is farther from the f3 pawn.
step.d_pawnFirst.m3: 2.a5. One more step. If the black king does not leave now, the pawn queens.
step.d_pawnFirst.m4: 2...Kd5. It goes after the a-pawn and gives up the kingside.
step.d_pawnFirst.m5: 3.a6. The pawn is two steps from queening: the black king has to step into c6 now, or it queens.
step.d_pawnFirst.m6: 3...Kc6. The black king catches the pawn, four files away from g5.
step.d_pawnFirst.m7: 4.Kxd4. Now is the time. The black king still needs two moves to capture the a-pawn, and my king goes via e5 and f5 to g5.
step.pawnFirstMove: Your turn, in the same position. Which pawn moves first, and when does the king capture d4?
step.pawnFirstMove.hint: The a-pawn first. The d4 pawn is not going anywhere.
step.pawnFirstMove.done: That's it: the pawn reached a6 before the king captured d4, and the black king is tied to the a-file.
step.escortWhy: So far the decoy was far from the black king, and my king could let it go. Here the decoy on f5 is close to the black king, and my king on g6 protects it and watches f6. If my king leaves, for example 1.Kh6?, then 1...Kf6 and the pawn falls. So the pawn advances with check, making the black king lose a tempo, and my king always stays beside it.
step.d_escort: Watch the pawn walk with the king beside it, one step at a time.
step.d_escort.m1: 1.f6+. The decoy advances with check. The black king has to leave e7, and it cannot capture on f6: my king protects it.
step.d_escort.m2: 1...Kf8. The black king steps in front of the pawn.
step.d_escort.m3: 2.f7! The pawn moves again, still beside my king, which protects it. Now it takes e8 and g8 away from the black king.
step.d_escort.m4: 2...Ke7. The black king attacks the pawn, but cannot capture it: it is protected.
step.d_escort.m5: 3.Kg7! My king guards f8, and the pawn queens next move.
step.escortMistake: Now the natural mistake: bringing the king behind the pawn. After 1.f6+ Kf8 2.Kf5?, the black king comes back, 2...Kf7, and stands in front of the pawn. My king, behind it, can no longer drive it away, and it is a draw. The king goes beside the pawn, never behind it.
step.escortMove: Your turn, in the same position. Here the decoy on f5 is close to the black king, and your king stands beside it. Take the pawn forward with the king alongside.
step.escortMove.hint: Push the pawn with check and keep the king next to it.
step.escortMove.done: That's it. The most direct way is 1.f6+ and 2.f7! The black king cannot capture the protected pawn, and 3.Kg7! guards f8. 1.Kg5 and 1.Kg7 also win, because the king stays close to the pawn.
step.t_down: A study position by fabian1999, with the colours reversed. White is a pawn down: two against three. Even so White wins, but with one move only. Which one, and why?
step.t_down.hint1: Look at the queenside: two black pawns against one white. Can a single pawn hold both?
step.t_down.hint2: On the kingside each side has a passed pawn: yours on h3, Black's on f5. Which of the two is farther from the centre?
step.t_down.hint3: If the black king captures the h-pawn, how many moves does it need to get back to the queenside? And your king, starting from the centre?
step.downWhy: So far the other side had nothing to capture. Now it is two against three, and in the end it will be a race. First, 1.b5: this pawn alone holds back the a7 and b6 pawns. My h-pawn is the decoy, and a decoy needs no guard. That is why my king goes to the centre, to f4, and not to h4: from there it attacks f5 and stays close to the queenside. Only 1.b5 wins; every other move loses.
step.d_down: Watch the first half: being a pawn down does not matter, and the decoy drags the black king to the edge.
step.d_down.m1: 1.b5! One pawn holds two. Black's queenside pawns are stuck.
step.d_down.m2: 1...Kg7. The black king comes to the centre to defend f5.
step.d_down.m3: 2.Kf4. The king goes to the centre and attacks f5. 2.Kh4? to protect the h-pawn would only draw: the king would be stuck on the edge.
step.d_down.m5: 3.h4. The decoy starts to move. The black king cannot let it run.
step.d_down.m6: 3...Kg6. The black king moves next to the h-pawn without letting go of f5.
step.d_down.m7: 4.h5+! The decoy gives itself up with check. If the black king does not take it, it lets go of f5; and if it goes to f6, 5.h6 and the pawn runs to queen.
step.d_down.m8: 4...Kxh5. The black king captures, out on the edge of the board.
step.d_race: Now, after 4...Kxh5, count. My king captures f5 and from there needs four moves to reach b7, from where it attacks a7. The black king, on the edge, is much farther from the queenside.
step.d_race.m1: 5.Kxf5. Material is level. My king is on f5, in the centre; Black's is on h5, on the edge. Now the race begins.
step.d_race.m2: 5...Kh4. The black king cannot go through g4, g5 or g6: my king guards those squares. It has to go round.
step.d_race.m4: 6...Kg5. The black king follows, one step at a time.
step.d_race.m5: 7.Kd6. Two more moves to b7, and the black king is still on the kingside.
step.d_race.m6: 7...Kf5. It is still four files away from the b6 pawn.
step.d_race.m7: 8.Kc6. The b6 pawn is already attacked, and my king shuts off d5 and d6: the black king cannot get closer that way.
step.d_race.m8: 8...Ke5. Too late: it has to go round once more.
step.d_race.m9: 9.Kb7! The only winning move. The king attacks a7 and then b6, and the black king, still on e5, arrives too late to defend them. White started a pawn down.
step.downMove: Your turn, a pawn down. First the move that holds the queenside, then the king goes to work.
step.downMove.hint: The b4 pawn can tie down both black pawns with a single step. Then the king goes to the centre, after f5, and the h-pawn becomes the decoy.
step.downMove.done: Well done. The queenside is locked, the king is in the centre and the h-pawn is about to drag the black king. The rest is the race you counted.
step.t_defense: Now you are on the other side: Black has an outside passer on h4, far from your king. The black c4 pawn is right there, within your king's reach, for free. Capture it or not? And if not, where does the king go?
step.t_defense.hint1: Count how many moves the h-pawn needs to queen.
step.t_defense.hint2: After capturing c4, is your king still inside the h-pawn's square?
step.t_defense.hint3: The c4 pawn is not going anywhere. The h-pawn is.
step.defenseWhy: Until now the outside passer was yours. Now it belongs to your opponent, and what it wants is for you to get distracted. Count the square of the h4 pawn: it runs from h4 to e1. My king on d5 steps into the square via e4. If it goes to capture c4, it stays outside. The c4 pawn cannot run; the h-pawn can. First the outside passer, then the rest.
step.defenseMistake: Look at the mistake: 1.Kxc4? The c4 pawn has fallen, but my king has left the square. 1...h3 2.Kd3 h2 3.Ke2 h1=Q: the pawn queens, and the white king never got close. A pawn on c4 cost a queen.
step.d_defense: Now the right way. The king ignores c4 and goes straight for the h-pawn.
step.d_defense.m1: 1.Ke4! Straight for the h-pawn, and already inside the square.
step.d_defense.m2: 1...h3. The pawn runs: Black wants to see whether the king gets there.
step.d_defense.m3: 2.Kf3! The only move. 2.Kf4? would lose: after 2...h2 3.Kg3 h1=Q, the king arrives one move too late.
step.d_defense.m4: 2...h2. One more step: the pawn is one square from queening.
step.d_defense.m5: 3.Kg2. The king stands in front of the pawn: it will not queen now.
step.d_defense.m6: 3...Kf5. The h-pawn is lost, and the black king goes after White's central pawns.
step.d_defense.m7: 4.Kxh2. The outside passer has fallen, and the white king gets back in time to defend its pawns: a draw.
step.defenseMove: Your turn. Hold the draw: the king goes after the outside passer.
step.defenseMove.hint: Do not capture c4. The king steps into the h-pawn's square and gets in its way.
step.defenseMove.done: That's it. 1.Ke4, 2.Kf3 and 3.Kg2: all three moves were the only ones. The c4 pawn could wait.
step.t_prot: It is a position from Fine and Benko's manual, without the a-pawns. Black has an outside passer on h5. White has a passed pawn on c5, protected by the b4 pawn. So far the outside passer won or caused trouble. Who wins now, and how?
step.t_prot.hint1: Can the black king take the c5 pawn? Can it go away from it?
step.t_prot.hint2: If the black king cannot leave the c-pawn, who is free to go and get the h-pawn?
step.protWhy: The c5 pawn is protected by b4. The black king cannot capture it, and it cannot leave either, because the pawn would run. It is stuck. My king is not: it goes to get the h5 pawn. Here the outside passed pawn drags nobody; it becomes the target. One warning: no 1.c6? Away from its protection the pawn falls, and Black wins.
step.d_prot: Watch the white king go for the h-pawn. Notice that the black king can do nothing against the protected pawn.
step.d_prot.m1: 1.Kf4. The king heads for h5. The c5 pawn defends itself, with b4.
step.d_prot.m2: 1...Kd5. The black king leans on the c-pawn, but cannot capture it: b4 protects it.
step.d_prot.m3: 2.Kg5. The black king cannot go for the h-pawn: it would arrive too late, and the c-pawn would run.
step.d_prot.m4: 2...Kc4. Black tries something else: attacking b4, the protecting pawn.
step.d_prot.m5: 3.Kxh5. Black's outside passer has fallen. And if the black king captures b4? You play it.
step.protMove: Your turn. Go and get the h-pawn and, if the black king captures b4, know what to do.
step.protMove.hint: Your king goes to the kingside. The c-pawn stays where it is while b4 protects it.
step.protMove.done: Perfect. You captured the outside passer, and when the black king captured b4, 4.c6! ran on its own: the black king was outside the square.
step.t_pass: Black has the outside passer on h5. On the queenside it is two white pawns against one, and your b4 pawn can capture c5 or go forward. What do you do?
step.t_pass.hint1: After the trade on c5, how many passed pawns does each side have, and which one runs faster?
step.t_pass.hint2: What kind of passed pawn can the black king not capture?
step.t_pass.hint3: A passed pawn protected by another pawn cannot be captured by the king. Can your two pawns form that pair without trading anything?
step.passWhy: In the previous part the protected pawn was already there. Here you have to create it. If the b4 pawn captures c5, there is only one passer left against the outside one, and both run together. If it goes past, to b5, there is no black pawn in front of it or on the neighbouring files: it is passed. Then c4 protects it. The black king is tied to it, and my king goes to get the h-pawn.
step.d_passMistake: First, the natural trade: 1.bxc5? Count the steps of both pawns.
step.d_passMistake.m1: 1...h4. The outside passer goes at once: the white king is far from it.
step.d_passMistake.m2: 2.c6. My pawn runs too. The black king cannot catch it, but my king cannot catch the h-pawn either.
step.d_passMistake.m3: 2...h3. One step each, and neither king can catch the other pawn.
step.d_passMistake.m5: 3...h2. Both are one square from queening.
step.d_passMistake.m6: 4.c8=Q. I queen first, but the queen cannot reach the h-pawn.
step.d_passMistake.m7: 4...h1=Q. Queen against queen: a draw. The trade threw the win away.
step.d_pass: Now the right way: go past, do not trade.
step.d_pass.m1: 1.b5! The pawn goes past c5 and becomes passed.
step.d_pass.m2: 1...Ke5. The black king comes to the centre, closer to the queenside.
step.d_pass.m3: 2.c4. Now b5 is protected, and the c5 and c4 pawns block each other.
step.d_pass.m4: 2...Kd6. The black king goes next to b5, but cannot capture it.
step.d_pass.m5: 3.Ke4. My king leaves for the kingside: the b5 pawn defends itself with c4.
step.d_pass.m6: 3...Kc7. The black king stays close to the b-pawn, tied to it: if it moves away, the pawn runs.
step.d_pass.m7: 4.Kf5. The white king goes to capture h5, as against the protected pawn in the previous part.
step.passMove: Your turn. Create the protected passed pawn.
step.passMove.hint: Do not capture c5. The b4 pawn can go past it, and the c3 pawn comes to protect it.
step.passMove.done: That's it: 1.b5 and 2.c4. The protected passer is ready, and the black king cannot leave it.
step.t_fischer: Denver, 1971, fifth game of the Candidates semi-final: Fischer, with White, against Bent Larsen. After 36.Rxa5 Rxa5 37.Bxa5 Bxb2 38.a4 Kf8, the rooks are gone and the a4 pawn is passed, far from everything. Each side has a bishop and three pawns. What should Fischer do with his bishop?
step.t_fischer.hint1: Picture the board without the bishops: what ending is left, and who has the outside passer?
step.t_fischer.hint2: In a pawn ending, the black king would have to run after the a-pawn. And the white king?
step.t_fischer.hint3: Trading pieces helps the side that is better in the pawn ending. How can you offer the trade without losing anything?
step.fischerTrade: 39.Bc3! Fischer offered the bishop trade, and Larsen accepted: 39...Bxc3 40.Kxc3 Ke7. Without the bishops, a pawn ending with level material is left, and the a-pawn is the outside passer: the plan from the first part. With the bishops on the board, Black could leave the bishop to watch the pawn; without it, the black king has to go in person. Before pushing the pawn, Fischer brings the king to the centre.
step.fischerEnd: 41.Kd4 Kd6 42.a5 f6 43.a6 Kc6 44.a7 Kb7. The black king is stuck on b7, guarding a8. 45.Kd5 h4 46.Ke6, and Larsen resigned: the white king will capture Black's kingside pawns, and the black king, even if it captures the a7 pawn, is too far away to defend them. Fischer did not even need to queen, and he won that match 6–0.
step.recap: This is the game position with both kings already in the centre, before the a-pawn moves, and without the h-pawns. Before you play, the three rules of this lesson. First: in a pawn ending, look for the most distant passed pawn; it is often worth more than an extra pawn. Second: use it as a decoy. Take it as far as you can while the target cannot run, and only then send the king to the other side, counting the race. Third: on the other side, go after it at once; and if you can create a protected passer, it beats the outside one.
step.finish: Now play this position to the end, like Fischer. Drag the black king with the a-pawn and go and capture the pawns on the other side.
ex.e11: The h-pawns are blocked, and your d5 pawn is passed. Where does the king go? Find the winning move.
ex.e11.hint: The d5 pawn can be the bait. While the black king goes to take it, where does your king need to be?
ex.e11.solution: 1.Kd4! The king still protects d5 and already points at e5, f5, g6 and h6. The black king will take the d-pawn, and in that time the white king takes h6; the h-pawn queens. Any other move loses a tempo, and Black draws. After 1...Kc7, any king move wins; only 2.d6+? throws the win away. Position from La-Parca-Maldita's study (chapter "Final 83").
ex.e12: White has a passed pawn on a4, far from everything. Only one move holds.
ex.e12.hint: Before you take anything, count: can your king reach the a-pawn?
ex.e12.solution: 1...Ke4! The king goes straight after the a-pawn. 1...Kxe3? looks free, but after 2.a5 the black king is outside the pawn's square and cannot catch it. After 2.a5, 2...Kd5! (the only move) keeps to the shortest path. The outside passer only wins when the enemy king cannot get there; here it can, and the white king on d1 is too far from the black pawns.
ex.e13: White has the outside passer on a4. On the kingside you can trade pawns or go past them. What do you do? Find the winning move.
ex.e13.hint: After a trade, the a4 pawn becomes White's outside passer. What kind of passed pawn can the white king not take?
ex.e13.solution: 1...h4! and, after 2.Ke2, 2...g5! The h-pawn is passed and g5 protects it: the white king cannot take it, and the black king is free to go and get the a-pawn. 1...hxg4? only draws: the white king takes g4, and the a4 passer ties the black king down. Some king moves also only draw, and 1...Kf6, 1...Kf7 or 1...g5 straight away lose. Against the outside passer, the protected passer wins.
ex.e14: Position from the study "A Remote Passed Pawn" by Chessforall321. Find the right order of moves until the white king heads for the kingside.
ex.e14.hint: The c-pawn is your outside passer. The further up it is when the black king catches it, the more time your king gains.
ex.e14.solution: 1.c4!, 2.c5! and 3.c6!, and only then 4.Kxe4! The c-pawn drags the black king to c6; with the white king on e3, the e4 pawn cannot move and just waits to be taken. After 4...Kxc6, the white king heads for the kingside (5.Kf5 or 5.Ke5), takes h5 before the black king gets back, and the g-pawn wins. 1.Kxe4? straight away only draws: 1...Kg4!, the black king takes g3 and its h-pawn runs alongside yours. On the first four moves, only these win.
ex.e15: Position from the study "Ptotected and distant passed pawn" by slimshaggy. The g-pawn is your outside passer; d5 is the black passer. Beware of the natural move. Find the winning move.
ex.e15.hint: The white king has two jobs: the d5 pawn and the a5 pawn. The g-pawn only needs to drag the black king away, at the right moment.
ex.e15.solution: 1.Kf5! (1.Kh5?, protecting the pawn, loses), and after 1...Kd6, 2.g5! The pawn moves and the black king has to go after it. After 2...Ke7, 3.Ke5!, and after 3...Kf7, 4.Kxd5! The black king takes g5, but the white king is already on its way to a5: 5.Kc4 (or 5.Kc5, 5.Kc6) and, after 5...Kxg5, 6.Kb5! The white king takes a5 and the a-pawn queens. Apart from 5.Kc4, every move is the only one that wins.
ex.e08: The queenside pawns are blocked, and your g-pawn is the outside passer. What is the move, and what comes next? Find the winning move.
ex.e08.hint: The g-pawn can step forward with check. Then the white king has to stand next to it.
ex.e08.solution: 1.g6+! and, after 1...Kg7, 2.Kg5! The pawn advances with check and the white king protects it. The black king is tied to it, and the white king gains time to go to the queenside or escort the pawn. On both moves the alternatives only draw. Position from chessforall123's study.
key.decoy: Equal material, but White's edge pawn is far from everything. The black king has to chase it, and meanwhile the white king captures the black pawns on the other side. White wins, whoever is to move.
key.pawnFirst: White's edge pawn moves before the white king captures the blocked black pawn in the centre: every step takes the black king farther away.
key.down: A pawn down, White still wins: a single white pawn holds back Black's two queenside pawns, and the h-pawn becomes the outside passer that pulls the black king away. In the source, the position appears with the colours reversed.
key.defense: Now Black has the outside pawn. The white king has to go after it at once, without stopping to capture the pawn right next to it.
key.protected: The protected passer beats the outside passer: the black king cannot leave the protected white pawn, and the white king calmly goes and captures the black pawn on the other side.
key.pass: With two pawns against one, White does not trade: one pawn goes past the other and the second comes to protect it. A protected passed pawn beats the outside one.
key.fischerLarsen: Fischer against Larsen, 1971 Candidates: the white edge pawn drags the black king away, and the white king captures the pawns on the other side.
key.fischerSmall: Fischer against Larsen a little later, without the kingside edge pawns: the white outside pawn drags the black king away, and the white king captures the rest.
history: A passed pawn is a pawn with no enemy pawn in front of it or on the neighbouring files. When it is far from the others, out on the edge of the board, it becomes a decoy: the enemy king has to go and fetch it, and your king uses that time to capture the pawns on the other side. It is one of the most common weapons in pawn endings, and it often decides the game even with equal material. Nimzowitsch said the passed pawn has a lust to expand. The most famous example is from 1971: in the Candidates match in Denver, Fischer used an edge pawn as a decoy against Bent Larsen and won without ever queening; he took that match 6–0. But the outside passer has limits, and this lesson also shows when it is not enough.
practice: Now the real ending: an a-pawn and a g-pawn against two black kingside pawns, equal material. Drag the black king with the a-pawn and go and capture the rest. Choose the time control and go.
